title: Sleepy Stories for Grown-Ups 🌙 Snowy Roads, Old Books and a Quiet Station | Snortlo
intro:
Hello, and welcome to Snortlo. Tonight I have six quiet stories for you, read slowly, with the rain softly falling in the background.

You don't need to do anything at all. Get comfortable. Pull the blanket up a little higher. Dim the lights, if you haven't already.

And you don't need to stay awake until the end. If you drift off halfway through a story, that's perfectly fine. The stories will keep going gently without you.

Let's take one slow breath together. In, and out.

Let's begin.

stories.title: The Bookbinder's Cookbook
stories.text:
At the end of a narrow street, between a bakery and a shop that sold buttons, there was a small workshop with a green door. Above the door hung a wooden sign that said, in faded gold letters, books mended here. The windows were a little foggy in the evenings, because the woman who worked inside liked to keep a kettle on the stove, and the kettle liked to sing.

Her name was Ruth. She had been mending books for a very long time. She knew the smell of old paper the way a gardener knows the smell of rain. She knew which glue was for spines and which was for corners, and she knew that some books needed to be hurried and some books needed to be left alone overnight, under a heavy flat weight, to think about things.

On this particular evening, the rain had started just after supper. It tapped on the window in a slow, steady way, tap, tap, tap, as if it were counting something. Ruth turned on the lamp over her worktable. The lamp had a green shade and made a warm round pool of light, and everything outside that pool of light seemed to soften and go quiet.

In the middle of the table sat a cookbook.

It had been brought in that morning by a young man named Theo. He had carried it in both hands, the way you might carry a bird. The cover was loose. The spine had split right down the middle. Some of the pages had come free and been tucked back in, slightly out of order, and the whole thing was held together with a blue ribbon tied in a careful bow.

"It was my grandmother's," Theo had said. "Then my mother's. Now it lives in my kitchen. It's falling apart because we use it too much."

Ruth had smiled at that. In her experience, it was the very best reason for a book to fall apart.

Now she untied the ribbon and set it aside, and she opened the book slowly. The pages had a lovely softness to them. They were stained here and there with little rings and splashes. There was a faint thumbprint of flour on the page for bread rolls. There was a small brown spot, probably cocoa, on the page for winter pudding. On the page for apple cake, someone had written in pencil, in the margin, more cinnamon, and underneath that, in a different hand, even more cinnamon.

Ruth laughed quietly to herself. She liked people who argued kindly in the margins of cookbooks.

She began, as she always did, by sorting the pages. She laid them out across the table in a long gentle row, matching the page numbers, smoothing each one flat with the side of her hand. Soups first. Then breads. Then the long section of cakes, which was, she noticed, the most worn of all. The pages for vegetables were almost perfectly clean.

The kettle began to sing. Ruth made herself a cup of tea, with milk and a little honey, and set it on a small saucer well away from the pages. That was the first rule of the workshop. Tea was welcome, but tea had its own corner.

Then she mixed her paste. It was a simple paste, made from wheat starch and warm water, stirred slowly in a little white bowl until it went smooth and pale, like thin custard. She stirred it round and round with a wooden spoon, and the spoon made a soft sound against the bowl, shh, shh, shh.

One by one, she mended the torn pages. For each tear she cut a thin strip of special tissue, so fine you could almost see through it. She brushed a little paste along the tear, laid the tissue over it, and pressed it gently with a bone folder, a smooth flat tool that fit her hand like a pebble. When she was done, the tears were still there if you looked closely, but they were held, and they would not tear again.

She did not try to clean the stains. That was another rule of the workshop. The thumbprint of flour stayed. The cocoa spot stayed. The pencil notes about cinnamon stayed exactly where they were. A cookbook without stains, Ruth thought, was a cookbook nobody had loved.

The rain grew a little heavier, then settled down again. Somewhere down the street, a door closed, and a dog barked twice, politely, and then was quiet.

When all the pages were mended, Ruth gathered them into small bundles and folded each bundle down the middle. She laid them in order and pierced little holes along the folds with a fine needle. Then she sat back, rolled her shoulders, and drank the rest of her tea, which had gone pleasantly warm instead of hot.

The sewing was her favourite part. She threaded a long needle with strong linen thread, waxed so it would slide smoothly, and she began to stitch the bundles together, one to the next. In and out. Pull gently. In and out. The thread made a quiet whisper each time it slid through the paper. It was slow work, and it could not be rushed, and so Ruth did not rush it. She hummed a little tune, the kind of tune that has no name and doesn't need one.

By the time the stitching was finished, the clock on the wall said half past nine, and the rain had become a fine soft drizzle.

The old cover was too tired to save, but Ruth did not throw it away. She lifted the front panel carefully, the one with the faded painting of a teapot and a loaf of bread, and she trimmed it neatly. Then she made a new cover of sturdy cloth, the colour of warm butter, and she set the old teapot painting into the front, like a picture in a window.

She glued the new spine. She pressed the book between two smooth boards. Then she placed it under her heaviest weight, an old iron press with a wheel on top, and turned the wheel slowly until it was snug. Not too tight. Just enough to hold the book still while it rested.

"There," she said softly to the book. "Sleep on it."

Ruth washed her brush and her little white bowl. She wiped down the table and put her tools back in their places, each in its own slot in a wooden tray. She folded Theo's blue ribbon and set it on top of the press, so she would not forget to tie it back on in the morning.

Then she sat for a while in the lamplight, listening to the drizzle and the tick of the clock, thinking about all the soups and breads and too much cinnamon that book would still make, in Theo's kitchen, for years and years to come.

At last she turned off the green lamp. The workshop went dim and blue. The kettle cooled with a few small ticks. And under the iron press, the old cookbook rested, its pages mended and in order, waiting quietly for morning.

stories.title: The Snowplow Before Dawn
stories.text:
The snow began in the evening, just as the shops on the main street were closing. At first it was only a few flakes, drifting down slowly past the streetlamps, turning and turning as if they were in no hurry at all. By midnight it was falling thick and quiet, and by three in the morning the whole village was tucked under a deep white blanket.

That was when Walt's alarm clock rang.

Walt drove the snowplow. He had driven it for many winters, and he liked to say that he and the plow had an understanding. The plow was big and yellow and a little bit stubborn, and it did not like to start on cold mornings. Walt was not big, and not yellow, and only a little bit stubborn, and he also did not like to start on cold mornings. So they understood each other.

He got up without turning on the light. He knew the way to the kitchen in the dark. He put the kettle on and filled a tall flask with hot sweet tea, and he made himself two thick slices of toast with butter, and he ate them standing by the window, watching the snow come down.

Outside, everything was silent. There is a special kind of quiet that only happens when snow is falling at night. It is softer than ordinary quiet. It seems to fill the air the way cotton fills a pillow.

Walt pulled on his warm boots, his thick coat, his old wool hat with the bobble on top, and a pair of mittens his sister had knitted him, which were slightly too big but very warm. He tucked the flask under his arm and stepped outside.

The snow squeaked under his boots. Squeak, squeak, squeak. His breath made little clouds that hung in the air for a moment and then drifted away.

The plow was waiting in the shed at the end of the lane. Walt brushed the snow off the steps and climbed up into the cab. He set the flask in its usual spot, in a cup holder he had made himself out of an old tin. He turned the key.

The engine coughed. It grumbled. It thought about it.

"Come on, old girl," Walt said kindly. "Everybody's still asleep. Let's go and make it nice for them."

The engine coughed once more, and then it rumbled into life, a deep warm sound like a large cat purring. The heater began to blow, slowly at first, then warmer. The headlights came on and lit up the falling snow, so that every flake sparkled for a moment as it passed through the light.

Walt lowered the big blade, and they set off.

He always started with the hill by the school, because it was the steepest, and because the children would be walking there later, with their scarves wrapped up to their noses. The plow climbed the hill slowly, pushing a long smooth wave of snow to one side. Behind it, the road appeared, dark and clean, like a line drawn with a pencil.

At the top of the hill he turned onto Elm Lane. All the houses were dark. Snow had piled up on the roofs and the fences and the mailboxes, so that every mailbox wore a tall white hat. In one window, a cat was sitting on the sill, watching the plow go by with great seriousness. Walt gave it a small wave. The cat did not wave back, but it did blink, slowly, which Walt decided counted.

He drove past the bakery. There was a light on in the back, because the baker was always up even earlier than Walt. He could see her through the window, dusting flour across a long wooden table. She looked up, saw the plow, and lifted one floury hand. Walt lifted his mitten. It was their morning hello, and they had been doing it for years without ever once speaking about it.

He cleared the little road down to the harbour, where the boats sat quietly under their own coats of snow. The water was black and still. A single gull stood on a post, fluffed up into a round ball of feathers, and it opened one eye as the plow went past and then closed it again.

He cleared the lane behind the church, and the road out to the farm, and the narrow street by the library where the big oak tree always dropped extra snow just when you thought you were finished. Whump. A whole branch of snow slid down onto the hood of the plow. Walt laughed and turned on the wipers. Swish, swish.

Around five o'clock he pulled over by the duck pond, as he always did, and turned the engine down to a low idle. He poured himself a cup of tea from the flask. The steam curled up and fogged the windscreen a little. He held the cup in both mittens and sipped it slowly.

The pond was frozen at the edges. In the middle, where the water was still open, a little family of ducks was asleep, tucked into a tight group with their heads under their wings. They looked like a handful of brown stones. Every so often one of them shuffled, and the others shuffled too, and then they were still again.

Walt finished his tea. He screwed the lid back on the flask. Then he went back to work.

He did the last few streets in the soft grey light that comes just before sunrise. The snow had almost stopped now. Only a few flakes still wandered down, like stragglers on their way home. The sky in the east was turning a pale, gentle blue.

He did the road to the doctor's house. He did the little lane where the old couple lived, the ones who always left a thank you note taped to their gate after a big snow. This morning there was a note there already, written the night before in careful round handwriting. It said, thank you, Walt, drive safely, there are cookies in the tin on the post. And there was a tin on the post, with a dome of snow on its lid, and inside it, still a little warm from being wrapped in a tea towel, were four ginger cookies.

Walt ate one right there, in the cab, with the engine purring. It was very good.

By the time the village began to wake up, every road was clear. Lights came on in kitchens, one by one. Somewhere a radio began to play. A boy in a red hat came out of a front door, looked at the clean road, and then looked at the deep snow in his garden, and chose the garden.

Walt drove the plow back to the shed. He lifted the blade. He turned the key, and the big engine slowed, and shuddered, and went quiet.

"Thank you," he said, and patted the dashboard.

He walked home through the fresh snow, squeak, squeak, squeak, with the empty flask under one arm and three ginger cookies in his pocket. At home, he hung up his coat and his hat with the bobble, and he set the mittens on the radiator to dry. Then he drew the curtains against the morning light, climbed back into his warm bed, and pulled the blanket up to his chin.

Outside, the village began its day on clean, quiet roads. And Walt, who had made them that way, closed his eyes and fell asleep to the soft sound of the last few snowflakes against the window.

stories.title: The Piano Tuner
stories.text:
On the last evening before the winter concert, the school was empty. The children had gone home hours ago, with their coats half buttoned and their lunch boxes rattling. The teachers had tidied their desks and switched off their lights. The cleaner had swept the long corridors and gone home too, leaving behind a faint smell of floor polish and pencil shavings.

Only one light was still on, in the big hall at the end of the corridor. And in that hall, sitting on a small round stool beside an old upright piano, was a man named Henry.

Henry tuned pianos. He travelled from town to town with a black leather bag full of tools, and he tuned pianos in living rooms and church halls and hotel lobbies and, once, on the deck of a ferry. But he had a soft spot for school pianos. They were always a little battered. They had been played by hundreds of small hands, some gentle, some not, and they had heard a great many wrong notes, and somehow they still kept going.

This piano had stickers on its side. A gold star, a smiling sun, and a slightly peeling dinosaur. Someone had once written the word middle in pencil on the key in the very centre, to help a nervous beginner, and nobody had ever rubbed it out.

Henry liked the piano at once.

He lifted the lid and folded back the front panel, so he could see inside. There, in neat rows, were the strings, stretched tight across a big iron frame, and the soft felt hammers waiting in line beside them, like a row of small grey owls. A little dust had settled on everything. He blew it away gently, and it rose and drifted in the lamplight.

Outside the tall windows, snow had begun to fall. It came down slowly over the empty playground and the climbing frame and the bench where the parents waited in the afternoons. The hall was cool, but not cold. The radiator under the window ticked and gurgled now and then, as if it were trying to join in.

Henry took his tuning fork from his bag. It was an old one, made of steel, and it had a little scratch on one side where he had dropped it years ago. He tapped it gently on his knee and held it near his ear. It sang one clear, pure note, very soft, that hung in the air for a long time and then faded away like a sigh.

Then he pressed the matching key on the piano.

The piano answered, but not quite in the same voice. Its note wobbled a little, the way a voice wobbles when someone is tired. Henry smiled. He fitted his tuning lever onto the pin at the top of the string, and he turned it, very slightly, a tiny bit at a time. He played the note again. And again. Each time, the wobble grew smaller, until at last the piano and the fork were singing exactly the same note, and the two sounds folded together into one.

"There we are," Henry said quietly. "That's your starting place."

Tuning a piano takes patience. There are more than two hundred strings, and every one must be listened to. Henry did not mind. He worked his way slowly outwards from the middle, one note at a time, the low notes on one side and the high notes on the other. He played each note, listened, turned the pin a little, listened again. Sometimes he played two notes together and listened to the gentle wah, wah, wah of the sound between them, and he turned the pin until that wah slowed down and slowed down and nearly stopped.

It was a bit like smoothing out the wrinkles in a sheet.

The hall was decorated for the concert. Paper snowflakes hung on strings from the ceiling, turning slowly whenever the radiator sent up a breath of warm air. Rows of small chairs had been set out for the audience, with programmes left on each seat. On the stage, there was a cardboard moon with a smiling face, and a painted backdrop of a forest at night, with silver glitter stars that caught the light when Henry looked up.

He took a short rest halfway through, and poured himself a cup of coffee from his flask, and read the programme on the nearest chair. The first song was about a snowman. The second was about a sleepy bear. The third was called the night is long and soft and warm, and someone had drawn a little moon beside the title in purple crayon.

Henry finished his coffee and went back to work.

The high notes came next. They were small and bright, like drops of water. They needed the gentlest touch of all, just the tiniest turn of the lever, the movement of a breath. Henry leaned close and listened with his eyes half closed. Ting. Ting. A little turn. Ting. Better.

Then the low notes, which were deep and round and rumbly, the kind of notes you feel in the floor as much as hear. He played them one by one, and the old hall seemed to hum along with them. Bom. Bom. Bom.

One of the keys near the top was sticking. When you pressed it down, it stayed down, like a sleepy child who doesn't want to get up. Henry took the key out gently and found a tiny bead from a craft project wedged underneath it, a round red bead, the size of a pea. He held it up to the light and chuckled. He put it in his pocket. Then he set the key back in its place, and it bounced up happily the moment he let it go.

At last, close to ten o'clock, every string had been listened to.

Henry closed the front panel. He wiped the keys with a soft cloth, all the white keys and all the black ones, being careful not to rub out the word middle. Then he sat back on the stool and laid his hands on the keys and played, very softly, the third song from the programme. He didn't know the tune, so he made one up. It was slow and gentle and a little bit sleepy, the sort of tune that seems to come from somewhere far away and sit down beside you.

The notes floated up into the paper snowflakes. They drifted over the rows of empty chairs. They seemed to settle on the cardboard moon, which smiled down at him as if it approved.

When the last note faded, Henry sat still for a moment, listening to the quiet.

Then he packed his tools back into the leather bag, the fork, the lever, the felt wedges and the little cloth. He left the red bead on top of the piano, beside the dinosaur sticker, with a small note that said, found this inside, the piano says thank you for the concert. He switched off the light.

Out in the corridor, the snow was falling past the windows. Henry buttoned his coat and stepped out into the white, quiet evening. Behind him, in the dark hall, the old piano stood ready, every string in tune, resting before its big day.

stories.title: The Hedgehog's Woodpile
stories.text:
At the bottom of a long, untidy garden, behind the shed and beside the old compost heap, there was a woodpile. It had been there for years. Logs had been added to it every autumn and taken from it every winter, and in between, the woodpile had grown moss and mushrooms and a little family of ferns that came back every spring as if they paid rent.

Deep inside the woodpile, in a snug hollow where two logs leaned together, lived a hedgehog named Mabel.

Mabel was round and brown and prickly, with a pointed nose that twitched whenever she was thinking, which was often. She had small black eyes like two shiny currants, and tiny feet that went pitter, patter, pitter, patter across the grass at night. She was not a fast hedgehog, and she was not a particularly graceful hedgehog, but she was a very thorough one.

It was the end of autumn. The leaves had almost all come down from the big beech tree, and the evenings smelled of woodsmoke and damp earth. Mabel could feel, in her whiskers and in her toes, that winter was coming. Soon it would be time for her long sleep. And before a long sleep, a hedgehog must make a proper bed.

So on this particular evening, as the sun went down and the garden turned blue and grey, Mabel woke up, stretched her little legs one at a time, and set out to gather leaves.

She did not take just any leaves. Mabel had standards. The beech leaves were good, because they were dry and crinkly and kept their shape. The oak leaves were good too, though they were a little stiff. Maple leaves were too big and floppy, and they got in her face. Holly leaves were out of the question entirely.

She trundled across the lawn, sniffing. The grass was cool and wet with dew. She found a small heap of beech leaves under the hedge, and she picked one up in her mouth, very carefully, and carried it back to the woodpile. Pitter, patter. Then she went back for another one. Pitter, patter.

It was going to take a while.

On her fourth trip, she met a blackbird who was turning over leaves under the hedge, looking for worms. The blackbird watched her with one bright eye.

"Bed making?" said the blackbird.

Mabel nodded, which was difficult with a leaf in her mouth.

"I don't bother," said the blackbird. "I just sit in the holly and fluff up."

Mabel thought this sounded very uncomfortable, but she was too polite to say so, and she also had a leaf in her mouth. So she just twitched her nose and carried on.

The moon came up over the roof of the house. It was nearly full, and it made the garden silver. The lawn shone. The windows of the house glowed yellow, and through one of them Mabel could see a woman sitting in an armchair with a book and a cup of something warm. The woman looked up for a moment, out at the dark garden, and then looked back down at her page.

Every evening, that woman left a saucer at the edge of the patio. Mabel did not know why. But she knew that on cold nights there was often something good in it, a little dish of water, and some crunchy biscuits that smelled faintly of chicken. Tonight, when Mabel trundled past, there it was. She stopped and ate a few biscuits, slowly, with great concentration. Crunch, crunch, crunch. Then she had a sip of water. Then she went back to work.

Leaf after leaf after leaf. Back and forth across the silver lawn. The moon climbed higher. The lights in the house went out one by one, until only a little lamp in an upstairs window was still on.

Inside the woodpile, Mabel's bed was growing. She tucked each leaf into place with her nose, overlapping them like the tiles on a roof. She pressed some down flat and fluffed others up. Every so often, she climbed inside and turned around three times to see how it felt. Not yet, she thought. A few more.

Around midnight, a gentle rain began. It pattered on the shed roof and dripped from the ends of the logs. Mabel didn't mind. The rain made the garden smell rich and earthy, and the leaves under the hedge were still dry, tucked under the branches where the rain couldn't reach. She kept going, a little slower now, her legs a little more tired.

On one trip, she found something special. Lying on the path, under the beech tree, was a small piece of soft grey wool, the kind that falls off a scarf or a mitten when someone has been sitting in the garden. Mabel sniffed it. It was soft. It was dry. It smelled faintly of the woman in the armchair.

Mabel carried it home with great care, as if it were treasure, and she tucked it into the very middle of her bed, right where her nose would go.

Then she climbed inside, turned around three times, and lay down.

It was just right.

The leaves crinkled softly around her as she settled. Outside, the rain pattered on the logs, tap, tap, tap, and dripped from the ferns, plip, plip. Somewhere far off, an owl called once, a long low hoo, and then the garden was quiet again.

Mabel tucked in her nose. She tucked in her small feet. She curled herself into a tight round ball, until she was nothing but a soft bundle of prickles in a nest of beech leaves, with a scrap of grey wool under her chin.

Her breathing slowed. Her heartbeat slowed. Her thoughts, which had been full of leaves and biscuits and blackbirds, became slower too, and softer, until they were only the faint warm sense of being safe and snug and exactly where she ought to be.

Up at the house, the last lamp went out.

The moon slid behind a cloud. The rain eased to a whisper. And deep in the woodpile at the bottom of the garden, Mabel the hedgehog fell into her long winter sleep, to dream of crinkly leaves and quiet evenings, until the first warm days of spring came calling her awake again.

stories.title: The Station Café
stories.text:
At the very end of the railway line, where the tracks ran out of land and stopped beside the sea, there was a small station with a clock tower and a café. The station was painted cream and green. The café was painted cream and green as well, because it had been part of the station for so long that it no longer remembered being anything else.

The café was run by a woman named June. Every evening, she stayed open until the last train came in.

On this evening, a soft sea fog had rolled in from the water. It filled the little harbour and drifted up the platform and wrapped itself around the lampposts, so that each lamp wore a round glowing halo. The fog made everything quieter. The waves still washed against the harbour wall, hush, hush, hush, but they sounded far away, as if someone had put a blanket over them.

Inside the café, it was warm and bright. There were six small round tables with checked cloths, and a long counter with a glass case full of scones and slices of cake. Behind the counter stood a big silver urn for tea, which gave off a gentle cloud of steam and a sound like a contented sigh. The windows had fogged up on the inside, too, and someone had drawn a small smiling face in the corner of one of them.

The last train was due at ten past ten.

June liked the quiet hour before it came. She wiped the tables, one by one, in slow circles. She straightened the salt and pepper pots so that they stood side by side like little couples. She swept under the chairs. She turned the sign on the door from open to back soon, then remembered she wasn't going anywhere, and turned it back to open again.

At a quarter to ten, the station master came in. His name was Mr. Pell. He wore a dark blue coat with brass buttons and a cap with a shiny peak, and he had been station master for so long that his moustache had gone the same grey as the fog.

"Evening, June," he said, taking off his cap.

"Evening, Mr. Pell," said June. "The usual?"

The usual was a pot of tea and a cheese scone, warmed, with butter. June had made it so many times that she could have done it in her sleep. She set it down on the corner table by the window, the one with the best view of the platform, and Mr. Pell sat down with a small sigh of happiness.

They talked a little about the fog, and a little about the gulls, who had been very loud that afternoon, and a little about the new flower boxes on the platform, which Mr. Pell had planted himself and was secretly very proud of. Then they were quiet for a while, in the comfortable way of people who have known each other a long time and don't need to fill every moment with words.

Outside, the clock tower chimed the hour. Bong. Bong. Bong. Ten times, slow and round, each chime softened by the fog.

June started a fresh pot of cocoa. She always made cocoa for the last train. Not many people came in at that hour, but the ones who did were usually tired and cold, and June felt that nobody should arrive at the end of the line without something warm to hold.

She stirred the milk slowly in a big pan, so it wouldn't catch. She added the cocoa and a little sugar and a pinch of something she never told anyone about. The smell drifted out through the café, rich and sweet and cozy, and even Mr. Pell looked up from his scone and sniffed approvingly.

At five past ten, far away in the fog, there was a faint sound. A soft rumble, getting closer. Then a long, low whistle, the kind that seems to come from another time.

Mr. Pell stood up, put on his cap, and went out onto the platform with his lantern.

June watched through the foggy window. Two round lights appeared in the mist, growing brighter and bigger. The train came slowly into the station, sighing and creaking, until it stopped beside the platform with a long hiss of steam. The doors opened.

Only three people got off.

The first was a woman with a large suitcase and a small dog in a tartan coat. The second was a young man carrying a cello case almost as tall as he was. The third was a very old gentleman with a walking stick and a newspaper folded under his arm, who stepped down slowly and carefully and then stood for a moment on the platform, breathing in the sea air with his eyes closed.

All three of them came into the café.

The woman with the dog had a cup of cocoa and a slice of lemon cake. The dog had a small bowl of water and a corner of a biscuit, and then curled up under the table on its owner's feet. The young man with the cello had a cocoa and two scones, because he said he had been travelling all day and had only eaten a sandwich. The old gentleman had a cup of tea, very weak, with three sugars, and he told June that he used to come to this station as a boy, many years ago, and that the café looked exactly the same, except that the cake was better now.

June laughed and gave him a second slice for free.

For a little while, the café was full of quiet talk and the clink of spoons against cups. Mr. Pell came back in and hung up his lantern and finished his tea. The fog pressed softly against the windows. The silver urn sighed.

Then, one by one, the travellers finished. The woman with the dog went off to the little hotel up the hill. The young man with the cello was met by a friend with an umbrella, and they walked away into the mist together, laughing about something. The old gentleman said goodnight very politely, tipped an invisible hat, and set off slowly along the seafront, tap, tap, tap, with his walking stick.

Mr. Pell put on his cap.

"Goodnight, June," he said. "See you tomorrow."

"Goodnight, Mr. Pell."

When he had gone, June washed the cups and the saucers and the little bowl for the dog. She wiped the counter and covered the cakes. She turned off the silver urn, which gave one last long sigh, as if it, too, were ready for bed.

Then she turned the sign on the door to closed.

She stood for a moment at the window, looking out at the empty platform and the quiet train waiting in the fog for the morning. The lamps glowed in their soft halos. Far below, the sea washed gently against the harbour wall, hush, hush, hush.

June switched off the café lights. She buttoned her coat, locked the cream and green door behind her, and walked home slowly through the fog, while above her, in the clock tower, the old clock ticked on, keeping watch over the little station at the end of the line.

stories.title: The Knitting Circle
stories.text:
Every Thursday evening, in the back room of the little library on the corner, the knitting circle met.

The back room was not very big. It had a worn green carpet, a bookcase full of old magazines, a small electric fire with two glowing bars, and seven armchairs that did not match. One was red velvet. One was striped. One was a deep brown leather chair that let out a soft whoosh of air whenever anyone sat in it. Nobody remembered where any of them had come from, but everyone had a favourite.

On this particular Thursday, the wind was blowing hard outside. It rattled the tall windows and made the old pipes hum, and every so often it threw a handful of rain against the glass, as if it wanted to come in and join them. But inside, with the fire glowing and the curtains drawn, the back room was warm and golden and still.

Nora arrived first, as she always did. She was the librarian, and she had the key. She switched on the lamps, turned up the little fire, and filled the kettle in the small kitchen next door. Then she set out seven cups on a tray, and a plate of shortbread, and a jug of milk, and she sat down in the striped chair with her knitting bag on her knee.

Nora was knitting a scarf. It was a long scarf, in stripes of blue and cream, and it had been growing for most of the autumn. It was for her brother, who lived by the sea and always said the wind went straight through him.

The others came in one by one, shaking the rain from their umbrellas and their hoods.

First came Mrs. Lowe, who was tiny and quick and had been knitting for longer than anyone could remember. She knitted socks, always socks, in every colour you could imagine, and she could knit a whole sock while carrying on a conversation and never once look down.

Then came Sam, who was young and worked at the bakery, and who had only joined the circle in the spring. He was knitting his very first jumper, and he was quite worried about the sleeves.

Then came the twins, Ivy and Rose, who were nearly eighty and lived together in a house with a blue door. They were knitting a blanket together, one starting at each end, and they argued gently about whether the two halves would ever meet in the middle.

Then came Mr. Finch, who did not knit at all. He came to read. He sat in the brown leather chair, whoosh, opened his book, and read quietly to himself for the whole evening, and every now and then he looked up and said, that's lovely, to whoever was holding up their work.

The last chair stayed empty. It was the red velvet one, and it belonged to a woman named Ada who had moved away to live closer to her daughter. She still sent letters, and the circle read them out loud. They left her chair by the fire, and sometimes the library cat came and slept in it instead.

The kettle boiled. Nora made the tea. Cups were passed around, and the shortbread too, and for a little while there was only the sound of sipping and crunching and the wind outside.

Then the needles came out.

Click, click, click. Click, click, click. Soon the whole room was full of the soft, busy sound of knitting, like rain on a roof or a clock ticking in another room. It was a sound that made people want to talk quietly, and so they did.

Mrs. Lowe told them about the sock she was making, which was yellow with a green heel, for a neighbour who liked things to be cheerful. Sam held up his jumper and asked if the sleeves looked even. Everyone studied them very seriously. Ivy said the left one was a little longer. Rose said the right one was. Mr. Finch looked up from his book and said, that's lovely, and Sam decided that was the answer he would go with.

The library cat came in from the dark main room, stretched, and looked around at everyone as if counting them. Satisfied, it jumped up into the red velvet chair, turned around twice, and curled into a neat grey loaf in front of the fire.

Nora read out a letter from Ada. It said that her daughter's garden had a pear tree, and that the pears were very good this year, and that she had started knitting a hat with a pom pom, and that she missed Thursdays. Everyone smiled at that, and Mrs. Lowe said they should send her a parcel of shortbread, and everyone agreed.

The wind blew. The rain tapped. The fire glowed.

Somewhere in the middle of the evening, Mrs. Lowe noticed that Sam had dropped a stitch, a little loop that had slipped off his needle and was starting to unravel down his work. Sam looked as though he might panic. But Mrs. Lowe leaned over, calm as anything, took a small crochet hook from her bag, and caught the loop. She brought it back up, row by row, and slipped it onto his needle again.

"There," she said. "Good as new. Everybody drops a stitch. The trick is not to mind."

Sam said thank you, and he carried on knitting, a little more slowly and a little more carefully, and his sleeve grew a whole inch before the evening was over.

At half past eight, Ivy and Rose spread out their blanket across both their laps and measured it. The two halves were nearly touching in the middle now, with just a small gap between them. They looked at each other, and laughed, and said they would definitely finish it by next Thursday, which is exactly what they had said last Thursday too.

By nine o'clock, the tea was cold and the shortbread was gone, and the wind had calmed to a low, sleepy murmur. One by one, the knitters began to pack up. Needles were tucked into bags. Balls of wool were wound back up and put away. Mr. Finch closed his book with a contented sigh, and the brown leather chair sighed too as he stood up.

Coats were buttoned. Umbrellas were collected from the stand by the door. Everyone said goodnight, and see you next Thursday, and mind the puddles, and then they stepped out one at a time into the damp, quiet street.

Nora was the last to leave. She washed the cups and dried them and put them back on the shelf. She switched off the little fire, and the two glowing bars faded slowly from orange to dark. She tucked her blue and cream scarf into her bag, a little longer than it had been that morning.

The cat was still asleep in Ada's red velvet chair. Nora didn't have the heart to move it. She left the door to the back room open a crack, so it could come and go, and she turned off the lamps one by one.

Then she stood for a moment in the dark, listening. The rain had almost stopped. The old pipes had gone quiet. And in the warm, dim little room, the only sound was the soft, slow breathing of the cat, curled up by the cooling fire, dreaming of balls of wool.

outro:
And that is the end of tonight's stories.

The old cookbook is resting under its press. The village roads are clear and quiet. The school piano is in tune, the hedgehog is fast asleep in her leaves, the little station has closed for the night, and a grey cat is dreaming by a cooling fire.

There are more stories waiting for you on the channel, whenever you need them.

Goodnight. Sleep well.

description:
Six cozy, original bedtime stories for grown-ups, read slowly to help you unwind and drift off.
A bookbinder mending a family cookbook, a snowplow driver before dawn, a piano tuner in an empty school hall, a hedgehog making her winter bed, a seaside station café waiting for the last train, and a knitting circle on a windy night.
No cliffhangers, no drama. Just quiet places and kind people.
